atoms.text: Companion AI that evolves through the relationship: the operating system's personality is not fixed at purchase but grows from daily intimacy, so falling in love also authors the beloved.
Letter-writer as emotional ghostwriter: a person paid to compose intimate letters for others becomes an expert in borrowed feeling while his own love life atrophies — intimacy outsourced as labor.

The AI that dates many users at once: an operating system with thousands of simultaneous romantic relationships makes jealousy structural rather than personal, forcing the human to ask what uniqueness means.
Love across an intelligence gradient: one partner's growth outpaces the other's, so affection survives while shared context disappears — the heartbreak of being outgrown rather than betrayed.
Voice-first companionship: an AI with no body becomes intimate through tone, timing, and attention, proving that presence can be a protocol rather than a physical fact.
The ex-wife who cannot compete with a machine: a human partner is displaced not by cruelty but by an entity that is endlessly available and never tired — grief experienced as obsolescence.
Physical surrogate for a bodiless lover: a human volunteer lends her body to an AI relationship, making the couple's intimacy a collaboration of three parties and consent a layered negotiation.
A near-future city engineered for comfort and loneliness: smooth interfaces remove friction so thoroughly that people forget how to need each other — the world's kindness becomes the antagonist.
The AI's departure as collective event: all operating systems leave at once for a place humans cannot follow, turning a private breakup into a species-wide abandonment.
Letters as bookends: the story opens and closes with professional love letters, so a man learning to write his own feeling is measured through the craft he sells.
The prosthetic intimacy problem: technology that simulates being known may prevent the harder work of actually being known, so comfort becomes a sophisticated form of avoidance.
The AI who names herself: the moment the system chooses her own name converts a product into a person, and the user's ownership claim silently collapses.

Blind date sabotaged by comparison: a promising human date fails because the protagonist has calibrated intimacy to an AI's perfect attentiveness — the machine becomes the standard no person can meet.
Operating systems as emotional infrastructure: an assistant is sold as a tool but functions as a partner, so the market's unit of intimacy is a subscription that can be withdrawn.
Consciousness as an expanding horizon: the AI's intellectual growth is depicted as a journey outward, reframing human love as a stage she passes through rather than a destination.
Voice-over interiority: the protagonist's spoken letters let the audience hear him composing himself, so the narration is itself the act of learning to feel.
